blocks.text: You spend a full day in a general practice surgery, watch 20 consultations, take one history yourself, and go home exhausted. A week later you cannot name one thing you would do differently. The experience happened; the learning did not. Turning placement time into learning needs three deliberate habits: taking and recording a good history, reflecting on what you saw, and asking for feedback.

blocks.markdown: Placements are where classroom knowledge meets real patients. But exposure alone does not make you a better clinician: **deliberate practice with feedback and reflection** does. This unit covers how to take a patient history under supervision and record it accurately, how to reflect on an observed consultation using a structured model, and how to obtain and act on feedback from a supervising clinician.

blocks.title: Reflective practice
blocks.text: **Reflective practice** is the habit of deliberately examining an experience, including your actions, thoughts and feelings, to understand it, learn from it and change future behaviour. It is expected of every doctor in the UK and forms part of annual appraisal and revalidation, so you begin building the habit as a student.

blocks.markdown:
### Taking and recording a history under supervision

Before you see a patient, agree with your supervisor which patient, how long you have, and what you are expected to do. Introduce yourself and gain consent (see the unit on ward professionalism), then use a **structure** so that nothing important is missed. Let the patient tell the story in their own words first, then clarify with focused questions, then summarise back.

blocks.caption: Structure of a medical history
rows: Presenting complaint (PC)
The main problem, in the patient's own words
One line, with duration
History of presenting complaint (HPC)
Onset, course, character, associated symptoms, relieving and aggravating factors, previous episodes
Chronological; include relevant negatives
Past medical and surgical history (PMH)
Previous illnesses, operations, hospital admissions
Note conditions relevant to the complaint
Drug history (DH) and allergies
Prescribed and over-the-counter medicines, doses, adherence, and allergies with the reaction
Record the reaction type; never leave allergy blank
Family history (FH)
Illnesses in relatives relevant to the complaint
Ages and causes where known
Social history (SH)
Home, occupation, smoking, alcohol, support, mobility
Quantify smoking and alcohol; note impact on daily life
Systems review (SR)
Brief screen for symptoms in each body system
Positive and relevant negative answers
Ideas, concerns, expectations (ICE)
What the patient thinks is wrong, what worries them, what they hope for
Often the key to a satisfying consultation

blocks.title: Turning a conversation into an accurate entry
blocks.prompt: A 62-year-old retired bus driver tells you: 'My ankles have been puffy for about three weeks, mostly by evening, and I get out of breath walking up the hill to the shops, which I didn't before. I sleep on three pillows now. I take a water tablet and a blood pressure pill, and I'm allergic to penicillin, it gives me a rash. I smoked 20 a day for 30 years but stopped five years ago. I'm worried it's my heart.' Write an accurate structured history.

steps.text: PC: ankle swelling and breathlessness on exertion for 3 weeks.

HPC: bilateral ankle swelling, worse by evening; new breathlessness walking uphill; now sleeps on 3 pillows (orthopnoea suggested). Ask and record relevant negatives such as chest pain, palpitations, cough or leg pain if elicited.
DH and allergies: a diuretic and an antihypertensive (names and doses to be confirmed from the patient's list or records); penicillin allergy, reaction rash.
SH and risk factors: ex-smoker, 20 cigarettes a day for 30 years (30 pack-years), stopped 5 years ago; retired bus driver. Alcohol and home circumstances to be asked.

ICE: idea that the problem is with his heart; concern about this; expectation to be examined and told what is wrong. Present the case to the supervisor, state what you did not ask, and have the entry checked and countersigned.

blocks.answer: An accurate entry records the patient's own words, facts with duration, quantified risk factors, allergy with reaction and the patient's ICE, and notes what remains to be clarified.

blocks.title: Record what you were told, not what you assume
blocks.text: Never invent a negative finding you did not ask about, or fill gaps with 'normal'. If a question was not asked, write that it was not asked. Entries made by a student should be identified as such and checked by a registered clinician.

blocks.markdown:
### Reflecting on an observed consultation

A structured model keeps reflection from becoming a diary of events. Two commonly used models:

- **Rolfe's model**: *What?* (describe what happened), *So what?* (what did it mean, what did you feel and learn), *Now what?* (what will you do next).
- **Gibbs' reflective cycle**: description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, action plan.

Good reflection links the event to **specific learning**, such as a communication skill or a knowledge gap, and ends in a **concrete action** (for example 'practise open questions in my next three histories').

blocks.caption: Gibbs' reflective cycle applied to an observed consultation
rows: Description
What happened?
A GP saw a mother worried about her 3-year-old's fever, and used the child's drawing to start the conversation
Feelings
What were you thinking and feeling?
I felt anxious that I would miss something, and impressed by how the mother relaxed
Evaluation
What was good and bad?
Good: the mother's concern was named early. Less good: I did not notice the father's silence
Analysis
Why did it go that way? What does theory or evidence say?
Naming concerns early builds trust; non-verbal cues may signal unvoiced worries
Conclusion
What else could you have done? What have you learned?
I should observe the whole family, not only the speaker
Action plan
What will you do next time?
In my next three consultations I will note one non-verbal cue and check it with the patient

blocks.title: Reflecting using Rolfe's model
blocks.prompt: You observed a physiotherapist explaining home exercises to a 72-year-old man after a hip operation. He kept nodding, but later asked his daughter what he should do. Use Rolfe's model to write a short reflection.

steps.text: What? The physiotherapist gave six exercises verbally in a few minutes. The patient nodded, but afterwards asked his daughter for help.
So what? Nodding did not mean understanding. I felt uncomfortable because I also did not check he understood. This shows that teaching without checking can fail even when the patient seems agreeable.

Now what? In my own consultations I will use 'teach-back' by asking patients to tell me in their own words what they will do. I will practise this in my next three patient encounters and ask my supervisor whether it was clear.

blocks.answer: A good reflection moves from description to meaning to a specific, testable action, here the use of teach-back.

blocks.markdown:
### Obtaining and acting on feedback

Feedback is information about your performance given with the aim of improvement. It rarely arrives unprompted, so **ask for it**: choose a specific task, ask at a suitable moment (soon after, in private) and ask a focused question such as 'What is one thing I could improve in how I took that history?' Useful structures include **Pendleton's rules** (you say what went well, the supervisor says what went well, you say what could improve, the supervisor does the same, then agree an action plan) and workplace-based assessments such as the mini-CEX (mini clinical evaluation exercise).

items: Agree a specific focus before the encounter, such as 'open questions' or 'safe examination'.
Ask for feedback soon afterwards, in private, with a specific question.
Listen without defending; clarify what you heard and ask for examples.
Write down the feedback and identify one or two actions, ideally specific and time-limited.
Try the action in your next encounter and ask the supervisor to look for change.
Record the learning in your portfolio and review it at the end of the placement.

blocks.title: Feedback is a gift to act on
blocks.text: The value of feedback lies in what you do next. A student who says 'I was told to ask about allergies earlier, so in my next three histories I will ask within the first minute' shows both insight and change.

points: Take a history using a structure (PC, HPC, PMH, DH and allergies, FH, SH, systems review and ICE), record what the patient actually said, and have the entry checked by a registered clinician.
Use a structured model such as Rolfe's or Gibbs' to reflect on an observed consultation and end with a specific action.
Ask for specific feedback in private soon after a task, listen without defending, agree actions, and show change in your next encounter.

questions.stem: Which part of a history records the patient's own view of what is wrong, what worries them and what they hope will happen?

options.text: Ideas, concerns and expectations (ICE)
Systems review
Family history
Drug history

distractorRationale.a: Correct: ICE explores the patient's perspective.
distractorRationale.b: Systems review screens for symptoms in each body system.
distractorRationale.d: Drug history lists medicines and allergies.

questions.explanation: ICE captures the patient's ideas about the problem, their concerns and what they expect from the consultation. It often explains why the patient attended and shapes a satisfactory plan.

questions.stem: While taking a history, you forget to ask about allergies. When writing the entry, what should you do?

options.text: Go back and ask the patient, or record that allergy status has not yet been asked and tell your supervisor
Write 'no known allergies' to complete the form
Leave the allergy field blank without comment
Copy the allergy status from a different patient with similar details

questions.correctOptionText: Go back and ask the patient, or record that allergy status has not yet been asked and tell your supervisor

distractorRationale.a: Correct: accuracy requires you to ask or clearly record that it was not asked.
distractorRationale.b: Inventing a negative is dishonest and unsafe.
distractorRationale.c: A blank field can be misread as 'none'.
distractorRationale.d: Copying from another patient is a serious error.

questions.explanation: A history must reflect what was actually established. Recording an unasked question as a negative can lead to harm, such as a drug being given to an allergic patient.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best example of a stage-appropriate entry in Rolfe's 'Now what?' question?

options.text: 'In my next three histories I will ask about the patient's concerns within the first two minutes and ask my supervisor for comments.'
'The consultation was long and the doctor wore a blue shirt.'
'I felt nervous and the room was cold.'
'I will try to do better in future.'

questions.correctOptionText: 'In my next three histories I will ask about the patient's concerns within the first two minutes and ask my supervisor for comments.'

distractorRationale.b: This is a description (What?), not an action.
distractorRationale.c: This describes feelings (So what?), not an action.
distractorRationale.d: Too vague to act on or check.

questions.explanation: The 'Now what?' stage should end in a specific action that can be tried and checked. Vague intentions do not show how learning will change behaviour.

questions.stem: In Gibbs' reflective cycle, which stage asks you to consider why things happened as they did, and what theory or evidence helps explain it?

options.text: Analysis
Description
Feelings
Action plan

distractorRationale.a: Correct: analysis seeks to make sense of the situation.
distractorRationale.d: Action plan states what you will do next time.

questions.explanation: Gibbs' cycle runs from description to feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion and action plan. Analysis is where you ask why and link to evidence or theory.

questions.stem: After taking a history, you ask your supervisor, 'Was that okay?' and she replies, 'Fine.' What would most improve the feedback you receive next time?

options.text: Ask a specific question, such as 'What is one thing I could improve in how I asked about the patient's symptoms?'
Say nothing so as not to take up time
Ask a different supervisor and ignore the first
Wait until the end of the placement to ask

questions.correctOptionText: Ask a specific question, such as 'What is one thing I could improve in how I asked about the patient's symptoms?'

distractorRationale.a: Correct: focused questions prompt specific, usable feedback.
distractorRationale.b: Silence loses an opportunity to learn.
distractorRationale.c: This avoids rather than uses the feedback.
distractorRationale.d: Delaying reduces the value, since details are forgotten.

questions.explanation: General questions produce general answers. A focused question about a defined behaviour prompts specific feedback that you can turn into an action.

questions.stem: A supervisor tells you that your questioning was too closed and the patient did not get a chance to explain. You feel defensive. Which response best demonstrates acting on feedback?

options.text: Listen, ask for an example, agree a plan to start the next three histories with open questions, and ask to be observed again
Explain why the closed questions were necessary and that nothing needs to change
Accept it politely, but make no changes
Ask for feedback from a different supervisor who is more encouraging

questions.correctOptionText: Listen, ask for an example, agree a plan to start the next three histories with open questions, and ask to be observed again

distractorRationale.a: Correct: listens, clarifies, plans a specific change and seeks follow-up.
distractorRationale.b: Defending rather than listening prevents learning.
distractorRationale.c: Acceptance without action does not improve practice.
distractorRationale.d: Seeking only positive feedback avoids learning.

questions.explanation: Acting on feedback involves listening, clarifying, deciding on a specific action and checking that the change works. Defensiveness is normal but should not stop the process.

questions.stem: True or false: if you were not able to examine a patient's chest during a history, you may write 'chest clear' in the notes because it is probably normal.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Entries must record only what was actually done and found; writing an unperformed examination is dishonest and can mislead clinicians. If something was not done, state that it was not done.

questions.stem: Describe how you would take a focused history from a patient under supervision on placement and ensure it is recorded accurately.
markingGuide: Agrees with supervisor beforehand which patient and what is expected; introduces self and obtains consent
Starts with open questions and lets the patient tell their story, then clarifies with focused questions
Uses a structure: presenting complaint, HPC, PMH, drug history and allergies, family and social history, systems review, ICE
Summarises back to the patient to check accuracy
Records the history in clear language, in the patient's words where relevant, with dates, quantified risks and the allergy reaction
Records only what was elicited, notes what was not asked, signs the entry and gets it checked or countersigned by a registered clinician
questions.explanation: A structured, patient-centred approach makes sure that the important areas are covered, while honest recording and supervisor review keep the entry safe and accurate.

questions.stem: Choose a structured reflective model and use it to outline a reflection on an observed consultation in which you noticed a patient seemed worried but the doctor did not ask about it.
markingGuide: Names a recognised model such as Rolfe (What? So what? Now what?) or Gibbs
Description of the event factually without identifying the patient
Feelings and thoughts, and what the observer noticed
Evaluation and analysis: why a worry may go unexpressed, and links to ideas, concerns and expectations or communication evidence
Conclusion about what could be done differently, for example inviting concerns openly
Specific, time-limited action plan, for example asking about concerns in the next three histories under supervision
questions.explanation: A good reflection is more than description: it interprets the event and results in a testable change. Keeping the patient anonymous preserves confidentiality.

questions.stem: Explain how you would obtain useful feedback from a supervising clinician after a placement day and how you would act on it. Use Pendleton's rules or a similar structure in your answer.
markingGuide: Agrees a specific focus in advance and asks for feedback soon after the task, in private
Asks specific questions rather than general ones
Pendleton: learner says what went well, supervisor says what went well, learner says what could improve, supervisor adds, then agree an action plan
Listens without defending, clarifies, asks for examples
Writes down one or two specific, time-limited actions
Applies them in the next encounter, seeks follow-up and records learning in a portfolio
questions.explanation: Feedback has value only when it leads to change, so the process includes preparation, a structured conversation and follow-up. Specific questions and written actions turn comments into learning.
